title: Ashvamedhika
hook: the great sacrifice is finished and praised by all, and a mongoose with half a golden body says it isn't worth a handful of flour
tomorrow: the Pandavas' last journey, Yudhishthira's dog, heaven

segments.voice: Yesterday in Ashvamedhika, Arjuna was struck down by his own son at Manipura, and Ulupi's gem brought him back. Your line was the fight he demanded set him free. Did you receive a gift before testing it? Today, the last of this book. Day eight hundred seventy-two.

Gold handed out to the brahmanas, food for everyone, kings and sages crowding the grounds: the horse is home, the sacrifice is done, and everyone is saying there's never been a rite like it. And then, from a hole in the ground, out comes a mongoose. One side of its body is gold. It looks around at all this splendor and speaks, in a voice like thunder: this sacrifice of yours isn't equal to a little barley flour given away by a poor brahmana in Kurukshetra. The crowd goes silent. Today, the mongoose's story.
screen: `THE SACRIFICE IS DONE.` → `A MONGOOSE, HALF GOLD.` → `"NOT EQUAL TO A LITTLE FLOUR."`

segments.voice: The brahmanas ask the mongoose to explain, and it does. In Kurukshetra there lived a brahmana who fed his family by gleaning, picking up the grains left in the fields after harvest. A famine came. The family went hungry for a long time. At last the brahmana gathered enough barley to make a small amount of flour, and they divided it among the four of them: the man, his wife, their son and the son's wife. Just as they were about to eat, a guest arrived at the door, hungry. The brahmana welcomed him and gave him his own share. The guest ate it and was still hungry. The wife gave hers. Then the son gave his. Then the daughter-in-law gave hers. Every portion went to a stranger, while the family sat with nothing. Then the guest revealed himself: he was Dharma, righteousness itself, and he praised the gift as greater than great sacrifices, and the family was carried to heaven. The mongoose had come out of its hole as this happened. It rolled in the scattered flour, and the water where the guest had washed, and wherever the flour touched, its fur turned to gold. Half of it. Ever since, it says, it has gone from sacrifice to sacrifice, rolling on the ground, hoping to turn the other half gold. It just rolled in Yudhishthira's. Nothing changed. The epic puts this near the close of the book of a great royal rite. The verdict on the gold doesn't come from a priest. It comes from a small animal, and a handful of barley.
screen: `A GLEANER'S FAMILY IN FAMINE` · `FOUR SHARES, ALL GIVEN AWAY` · `THE GUEST WAS DHARMA` · then, large: `HALF GOLD, STILL ROLLING`

segments.voice: Sit, and rest your hands in your lap, palms up, as if holding a small bowl. Breathe in and think of the last meal you had. Breathe out and think of who else might have been hungry at that hour. Don't make it a guilt exercise. Just let the two thoughts sit side by side. Then think of one small thing, one portion, you could give away today, not grand, just real. If you pray, you can offer that intention in your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Ashvamedhika. The book of the horse sacrifice, which ends with a mongoose weighing it against a poor family's flour.
Your line: a handful of barley. Today, give one real portion of something, food, time, money, attention, to someone who needs it, without an audience. Day eight hundred seventy-two.

screen: `DAY 872 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE PANDAVAS' LAST JOURNEY, YUDHISHTHIRA'S DOG, HEAVEN.`

howItsDone: The story of the mongoose and the gleaner's flour closes the account of Yudhishthira's horse sacrifice in the Ashvamedhika Parva, and storytellers retell it to teach that a gift given in want outweighs great display.

match.prompt: the mongoose's story — tap the pairs.
pairs: one side of its body gold
gave every share of flour away
turned none of the fur gold

myth: it says the rite isn't equal to a poor brahmana's gift of flour.
the family gave their food while they were starving
it was a famine, and each gave their own share.
rolling in Yudhishthira's sacrifice turned the mongoose fully gold
nothing changed; it's still half gold.

fork.setup: you're the gleaner. after a long famine you have a little flour for your family of four. a hungry guest comes to the door. what do you do?
options: feed your family first; there isn't enough.
give the guest your own share.
fork.reveal: he gives his share, and when the guest is still hungry, his wife, son and daughter-in-law give theirs. the guest was Dharma.

original.note: nakula: a mongoose; the same word is the name of one of the Pandava twins.

trapdoor: what you thought: the grand horse sacrifice is the climax of the book.
what it means: the book ends with a mongoose saying a starving family's flour was worth more.
what a scholar hears: the epic lets a great royal rite be judged by a gleaner's gift, a theme of giving in want over giving in plenty.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Ashvamedhika Parva, the mongoose at Yudhishthira's sacrifice and the story of the gleaning brahmana of Kurukshetra and his gift of barley flour

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm in Ganguli: the mongoose's half-golden body, its thunderous voice, its claim that the sacrifice is not equal to a prastha of barley flour, and the order of giving (brahmana, wife, son, daughter-in-law).
Confirm that the guest was Dharma and that the family went to heaven, and that the mongoose rolled in the flour and the water the guest had used.
The text later identifies the mongoose with Wrath under a curse; this is left out and could be a future day.
Some recensions add a discussion of sacrifice and non-violence after this episode; not covered.
The note that nakula (mongoose) is also the twin's name is a standard lexicon meaning; please confirm wording.
The hook's "there's never been a rite like it" is reported speech of the crowd, not a claim; check it matches the text's praise of the sacrifice.
Editor pass: hook no longer opens 'The horse has...' like day 871; cut superlatives ('grandest', 'greatest', 'very end'), since further sections follow the mongoose story.
